data.sourceWord: Religious belief: sex within marriage only
data.targetWord: Most religious traditions teach that sexual relationships should only occur within marriage. This view protects commitment and family stability, and reflects the belief that sex is sacred.

data.sourceWord: Religious belief: LGBTQ+ views vary by tradition
data.targetWord: Religious views on same-sex relationships vary: conservative Christians and Muslims oppose them on scriptural grounds; liberal Christians and many Reform Jews affirm them as expressions of love and dignity.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.2 — religious beliefs about sexual relationships

data.targetWord: While most traditional religious teaching requires marriage before cohabitation, many liberal Christians and secular humanists accept cohabitation as a committed, loving arrangement that need not be formalised.

examples.en-GB: AQA Q1.3 — contrasting views on cohabitation

data.targetWord: Catholics and many evangelical Christians argue that cohabitation before marriage undermines the commitment marriage represents and separates the unitive and procreative purposes God intended for sexual union.

data.sourceWord: Gender discrimination — all created in God's image
data.targetWord: Religious believers argue that gender discrimination violates the belief that all people are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). Equal dignity before God means treating men and women equally in all areas of life.

Many traditions teach that justice requires opposing discrimination in all forms. 'There is neither male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.' (Galatians 3:28) supports full gender equality.
'There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.' (Galatians 3:28) — a key text used to argue for gender equality in Christian ethics.

data.title: Religious Approaches to Relationships and the Environment
data.sourceTitle: Religious Approaches to Relationships and the Environment
data.sourcePassage: Two of the most significant areas of ethical debate in religious studies involve relationships and the natural environment. On relationships, religious traditions affirm that human beings are made for loving community. Most teach that marriage between a man and woman is the ideal framework for sexual love and family life, because it reflects God's covenant relationship with humanity. However, views on cohabitation, same-sex relationships and divorce vary significantly between and within traditions. On the environment, religious believers draw on the concept of stewardship — the duty to care for the world God created and entrusted to human beings. The Hebrew Bible describes God seeing his creation as 'very good', and instructs humans to tend and keep the garden (Genesis 2:15). Islam teaches that humans are khalifahs (stewards) of the earth. The growing environmental crisis — including climate change and pollution — has led many religious communities to make environmental action a central moral priority, arguing that caring for creation is inseparable from loving God and neighbour.
